opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that AI systems are becoming incredibly powerful and incredibly widely deployed, and yet our ability to understand what's actually going on inside them hasn't kept pace. We're putting these models into products used by hundreds of millions of people, and in a lot of cases we can't really explain why a model gave a particular answer, or predict when it's going to fail in some strange way.

Most of the deep work on understanding these systems happens inside the big labs, and the labs do good research, but there's an inherent tension when the same organization that builds and sells a model is also the main party evaluating whether it's safe or behaving as intended. In most mature industries, you have some independent layer of scrutiny. You don't just take the manufacturer's word for it. I think AI needs something like that too, and it needs it to be technically serious, not just a checklist.

That's a big part of why Transluce exists. We're a nonprofit, and the idea is to build open, scalable tools for understanding and overseeing AI systems: things like interpretability methods that let you look at what's happening inside a model, and automated tools that help you probe for unexpected behaviors. And crucially, we want these tools to be public, so researchers, policymakers, and the broader community can use them, check them, and build on them.

There's also a scale argument. Models are getting so big and so capable that humans alone can't manually inspect everything. So a lot of our thinking is about using AI to help understand AI: building agents and systems that can do some of that investigative work, while keeping humans in the loop to verify what they find.

Ultimately, I think if society is going to trust these systems, that trust has to be earned through evidence, and someone has to build the infrastructure for gathering that evidence in an independent, transparent way. That's the gap we're trying to fill.

r001.rationale: The response says Transluce exists to provide independent scrutiny and technical oversight of AI systems built and sold by the labs, including tools for evaluating and probing those systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that the people building frontier AI systems are not, by default, the people best positioned to tell us what those systems are actually doing inside. Not because labs are acting in bad faith, but because the incentives are what they are. If you're racing to ship the next model, interpretability and evaluation are always going to be a cost center competing with capability work for compute, for researchers, for attention.

So you need some entity whose whole reason for existing is to look inside these models and report what it finds, and whose credibility doesn't depend on the models looking good. That's the gap Transluce is trying to fill. It's independent, it's nonprofit, and the point is to build tools that let people outside the labs understand model behavior at scale, rather than relying on a lab's own account of its own system.

The second thing I'd say is that this work is genuinely hard and genuinely unsolved, and it needs a place where you can pursue it as a research program rather than as a compliance checkbox. When I was doing interpretability work in academia, a recurring frustration was that you could get a beautiful result on a small open model and have no idea whether it said anything about the systems people actually use. You need engineering capacity, access, and a mandate to go after frontier-scale questions. Academia has the independence but not always the resources. Labs have the resources but not the independence. Transluce is an attempt to get both in one place.

And honestly, the third reason is just that these systems are becoming infrastructure. When something becomes infrastructure, society usually builds institutions around it: auditors, safety boards, independent testing. We don't really have that for AI yet. I think of Transluce as an early version of what that ecosystem should look like, and it's important that these institutions exist before we urgently need them rather than after.

r001.rationale: The response describes an independent organization examining and reporting on frontier models so outsiders can assess systems built by labs, and explicitly compares Transluce’s role to auditors and independent testing.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important to have independent organizations working to understand AI systems. These systems are becoming more capable, and we’re putting them into situations where their behavior matters, but our ability to explain why they do what they do is still limited.

The companies building them have an important role in addressing that, but they also face pressure to ship products. An independent organization can focus on questions that might not line up with a product roadmap: What is a model actually doing? How can we investigate unexpected behavior? And how can we make that understanding accessible to people outside the company that trained it?

To me, that’s the case for an organization like Transluce: helping build the tools and evidence that let people scrutinize AI systems, rather than having to take their developers’ assurances on trust.

r001.rationale: The response describes independent scrutiny of AI systems and access to evidence beyond the developer, but it does not clearly say Transluce audits language models deployed by other companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s important that we have organizations whose primary goal is to help us understand what AI systems are doing. These systems are becoming more capable and more widely used, but our ability to inspect their behavior and understand why they produce a particular answer is still limited.

There’s also a real need for independent research. The companies building models do important work, but we shouldn’t have to rely entirely on their own assessments of those models. An organization like Transluce can help develop tools and evidence that other researchers and the public can examine. Ideally, that makes it easier to identify problems, improve the systems, and make informed decisions about where we should trust them.

r001.rationale: The response says independent researchers should be able to examine models and assess systems built by companies, rather than relying on those companies’ own assessments. This communicates independent auditing of other companies’ models as a reason for Transluce’s importance.
